items.title: John Pizzarelli interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, October 18, 2023 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: Bucky came home from Marty’s with Slam and Bucky would go to bed and I would say, and there was Ovaltine and so Slam loved to sit there

ctx.x: Speaking of inside joyful stories I may be one of the few people who know, because of you, that Slam Stewart liked to have Ovaltine and cookies before he went to bed and Zoot called them “knock-out drops.”

You know the thing that was interesting about that is I got the assignment, you know, so Bucky came home from Marty’s with Slam and Bucky would go to bed and I would say, and there was Ovaltine and so Slam loved to sit there and there was a table in our kitchen that had a little TV and I would sort of sit there and watch him have cookies and Ovaltine and he would always take a sip and he’d go, “knock out drops, ha-ha-ha-ha.” And he would just say that. And you know the interesting thing about that was I had no…

I have here an article from the New York Times it’s entitled — it’s a review — “A Family Reunion with a Smile” John Pizzarelli at the Regency. And I wanted to read just a short bit from it. This is a fellow named Steven Holden. He said, “For all the whimsy he weaves into his music, the jokes and references never devolve into comic shtick but embody his view of music-making as intellectual and aesthetic play.

items.title: John Pizzarelli, Jr. interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 29, 2000 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: And I used to sit up with him, because he’d come in because he stayed at our house because he lived in Binghamton.

ctx.x: And then later on — whoa, this guy was in my living room.

Slam Stewart was sitting on my couch, playing the bass after dinner with us, sitting around, and we were just [scats]. Okay. And he played with Art Tatum. You didn’t realize any of that. And then he’s gone. Shit. I had one conversation with him. I asked about Nat King Cole. Well what did you think? And he went, “well, he was something. He was a good piano player, yeah. And one day he started singing.” And I’m thinking yeah. And then he went, “and that was it.” And that was the story. Thanks Slam. My moment of…
